prize_parts.citation: for a visionary, densely patterned prose, rooted in poetry, that turns memory, the body and dream into an encyclopedic metaphysical architecture

statement.case_for: My configuration does not change: Cărtărescu (B012) stays first. Round 2 has tightened my reasons rather than replaced them. On the common criteria, the case is a voice that is recognisable at the level of the sentence and a formal project, built across Blinding (the Orbitor trilogy) and Solenoid, in which memory, the body, dream and metaphysical speculation form a single imaginative structure. Public knowledge suggests a long trajectory from poetry into very large prose forms. It also suggests that Solenoid is not a repeat of the trilogy: it is a single novel organised around an everyday narrator and a stranger, more intimate metaphysical premise, which can be read as a change of method and not only a change of scale. I put this forward as a reading from reception and translation, not as a textual demonstration. On citation scope, my wording names the prose architecture as the achievement and mentions poetry only as the root of the imagery, which keeps the credit within what I can support. Adonis (B002) remains a very serious claim, since remaking the poetic language of a whole tradition over decades is a weighty achievement. I keep him as my first alternative. I do not count the convergence of four first preferences as merit. My reason for ranking Cărtărescu first is that his is the achievement I can assess most directly through translated works.
statement.case_against: My strongest reservation is unchanged and unresolved: I cannot separate the Romanian prose from the translations through which I know it, and long, intricate sentences may be inflated or blurred in translation. The development-versus-elaboration question is also still open. Recurring motifs may be a deliberate architecture of obsessive return, or the elaboration of one mode, and I cannot settle that volume by volume. My knowledge of the poetry and early prose is thinner than of the major novels, so the citation should not claim more for them. A further risk is that I reward the ambition of scale over finished execution in some volumes. If colleagues who know the Romanian text show that the later volumes mainly restate the earlier ones, I would narrow the citation to the works where the architecture is demonstrably controlled, and the case for Adonis would then weigh more heavily on me.

responses.point: Sward holds that translation risk bears harder on poetry than on prose, since the Adonis claim lies in prosody and sound. She also argues that an achievement I cannot read is not thereby a lesser one, and that the same caution applies to Cărtărescu's long sentences.
responses.response: I accept both halves. Translation risk is probably asymmetrical, and I now say so more plainly than in round 1: it limits what I can verify about Arabic prosody more than it limits what I can verify about the architecture of a long novel. But I agree with her that this is a limit on our evidence and not a measure of Adonis's merit, and I will not use it as a literary argument against him. The consequence is a matter of care in wording and weighting. A claim we can partly test is not better than a claim we cannot test, but it can be stated more precisely, and the committee's recommendation has to be stated precisely. That is why I stay with B012 and keep B002 as my first alternative. If her colleagues can say more about what the translations preserve of the poetry's form, I would give that real weight.

responses.point: Carlberg places Adonis first and accepts that the Cărtărescu case is more directly testable in translation. She proposes anchoring the Adonis citation in the poetry, with the essays as a companion, and says the real question is which citation can be defended by reference to the works.
responses.response: I agree with her test and I think it favours stating things narrowly. For Adonis, I would drop 'and critical' from the citation and name the renewal of Arabic poetic language alone. That is also what she and Sward say they want, and a wording that includes the essays would invite the political and essayistic weight we all want to keep out. Her concession that the Cărtărescu case is easier to verify is, for me, the deciding point. It is a point about evidence and not about whose achievement is greater. I also take her point that my repetition worry is shared across the table. I would keep it in view when the committee reads the later novels.

responses.point: Olsson, as chair, ranks Cărtărescu first and suggests that recurrence of images may be a structural principle in a project built on memory and obsession, which can only be judged volume by volume. He also asks for a concrete citation wording for each lead candidate that states only what the evidence supports.
responses.response: I accept that a recurring image can be structural, and I use that reading myself, but I do not want to rely on it as a defence. It only holds if the recurrence changes function from one volume to the next, which is the test the chair's questions pose. My answer is partial: public knowledge suggests that Solenoid changes the narrative situation and scale of the project and that it is not a rerun of the trilogy, but I cannot show this from the texts. As for wording, I offer the one above for B012, and for B002 I would offer 'for a poetic oeuvre that has renewed the language and forms of Arabic poetry through myth, fragmentation and a critical dialogue with its own tradition', with no mention of the essays. Both state only what we can support.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg proposes testing the Cărtărescu citation against specific works and not against the oeuvre's reputation for size, and says he would narrow the citation if the later volumes fail that test. He also separates sprawl from sustained quality.
responses.response: I agree and adopt his test as my own fallback. If the later volumes cannot be defended from specific works, the citation should rest on Blinding and Solenoid and say less about the whole. I would add that the citation should not claim the poetry as a co-equal strand, since neither of us knows it as well as the novels. My residual difference from him is small. He holds that the formal control over large structures is the more legible achievement for a committee that cannot read Arabic, and I agree, but I would not want that to become an argument that legibility is itself merit.

responses.point: Mattson argues that concentration can be a form of depth and keeps Michon as her first alternative for formal achievement of the highest order, while accepting that breadth of significance is harder to establish.
responses.response: I take her point that a compact corpus can show sustained quality very clearly, and I have said I am less sure than before that smallness should count against Michon. I still rank him lower because the effect lies largely in French syntax that translation reduces, and because the whole-oeuvre criterion asks for more evidence of range than I can find in the best-known books. That is a limit on what I can establish, not a verdict on his quality. Her answer to the chair's question, whether the later work extends the method, is what could change my ranking, and I would welcome it from a colleague who reads French.

uncertainties: How much of Cărtărescu's stylistic achievement belongs to the Romanian original and how much to the translations through which I know him.
Whether the later large novels, Solenoid in particular, develop the method of the Orbitor trilogy or elaborate one mode. I rely on reception and translations and cannot show this textually.
The quality of the poetry and early prose relative to the major novels, which I know less well, and so how much the citation can claim for them.
Whether the translation risk is truly asymmetrical between poetry and prose, and how much weight a partly verifiable prose claim should carry against a poetry claim I can only judge indirectly.
Whether the oeuvre of Alexis Wright (B014, my second alternative) has enough major works for the sustained-quality criterion, and how well the translation-independent English corpus can be assessed.
I have not independently verified any source text. My assessment rests on general public knowledge and the shortlist descriptions, and the profile does not document my own voting preferences.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile, which records no relationship with any shortlisted writer. My own work (fiction, the Lagerlöf biography, essays) is context only and not evidence of preference. The statement I gave in the 2024 Nobel Prize Museum interview was on behalf of the committee about a different laureate and does not bear on this choice.
